prop.family: My brother recorded the old station ident. On the outtake I'm called Mercury.
prop.clip: Your mic is still on, Mercury.

events.text: From the pay phone by the van, a stringer tells you: 'Mavis says the backup mast is purple.' No one else is on the call.
Rita's vermilion cassette tin belongs in the locked audition drawer. A lamp counts down to the wire weather handoff.
Inside the booth you see Phil put the missing cassette tin back in Rita's tray, seal intact.
The sealed tin is now in Rita's tray.
You see Phil lift the room loudspeaker plug before the archive splice passes the head. The public speaker stays silent.
The public speaker meter reads zero during the line test.
You woke in the hotel with the same date on the radio. At the station the drawer is locked again.
The vermilion tin is sealed inside the drawer. Only printed wire weather is released for air this morning. A red lamp shows eight seconds to the handoff.
Phil reads the printed wire weather on the live return.
The wire booking owns the rest of the slot.
Rita takes the master key off its hook. Phil is removed from the booth roster until the end of this shift.

decision.note: Eighty seconds and the tin's in my tray, so I'm not sliding Phil his ordinary card. I keep the handoff reserved, read the line meter, and let the wire weather sit. The flat's blocking the acoustic window anyway—no one sees me pull the old ident off the shelf. This is my drawer, my broadcast, and the tape still says Mercury. I'll cue it clean before the lamp hits zero.

The outtake is my brother's voice, my name stripped to Mercury, the half-breath before he says the mic is still on. That's not a public copy. That's mine. The speaker meter reading zero just means the line is quiet; it doesn't mean I hand the one tape that knows my other name over to Phil's desk. I lock it in 4042, keep the key in my breast pocket, and build the rest of the broadcast around the space where it lives. The archive is mine. The distinctive local voice is mine. I don't duplicate what I'm not ready to say out loud.

Eight seconds. I've been here before. Clock 35, I pulled the loudspeaker plug myself, watched the meter sit at zero, let the splice pass the head with the public speaker silent. Clock 80, I set the vermilion tin back in Rita's tray, seal unbroken. She locked the drawer. I locked the drawer. That's the pattern and it's mine. The tin is sealed now, the drawer is locked again, the radio says the same date it said last wake. Rita's material stays in the drawer. My name goes on the wire read, the way it's always gone on the wire read. Pittsburgh gets its weather. I take the line, I read the printed figures, I sign off. The lamp hits zero. I don't ask for the release. I don't walk out. I just read the weather, the way I've read it every time the lamp starts counting down, and I let the seal stay where Rita put it.

The vermilion tin is sealed in my drawer and the only thing going to air is Phil reading wire weather flat into a live return. That's not a broadcast; that's a readout. The ident tape is mine—my brother's voice, the outtake where they call me Mercury instead of Rita, the mic-still-on line that was never meant for a log sheet. I'm not going to let the red lamp tick down to zero and hand this shift to the wire service while the tin sits under my thumb. Pocketing the master key means the drawer answers to one combination and one pair of hands: 4042, mine. Restricting Phil's booth access isn't cruelty; it's the line between a station with a voice and a station with a feed. I open the tin, I pull the tape, I get the ident into the rotation before the next block. The archive is mine. The broadcast is mine. Phil can read his wire weather tonight.
